title: Writing text and formatted data to files
learningObjectives: Use fputc, fputs and fprintf for character, string and formatted output.
Check each output function's return value.
Use format specifiers that match the supplied argument types.
Understand that buffered output may fail during fflush or fclose.
Avoid writing untrusted text as a printf format string.

understand.concept: C streams support character, string and formatted output through fputc, fputs and fprintf. Output is commonly buffered, so a successful write call does not guarantee that data has reached the underlying file. Check the write operation and the later flush or close result. Treat format strings as trusted program data.
understand.whyItMatters: Checking write results prevents a program from reporting success when storage is full, a device fails or the stream becomes invalid.
understand.analogy: Treat the operation as a clearly specified contract between the program and its data.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's type, lifetime, I/O and object representation rules.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Character and string output

Use fputc to write one character and fputs to write a null-terminated string. Check for EOF or the documented failure result.

## 2. Formatted output

fprintf writes formatted data to a stream. Its conversion specifiers must match the types of the corresponding arguments. Use `%zu` for size_t and appropriate length modifiers for other types.

## 3. Buffering

The C library may buffer output. Errors can appear when the buffer is flushed explicitly or when the stream is closed. Check fflush and fclose when reliable output matters.

## 4. Format-string safety

Do not pass untrusted input as the format string. Use `fprintf(file, "%s", text)` rather than `fprintf(file, text)` when text is data.

## 5. Resource handling

Check fopen, every important write, and fclose. A program should not report a successful save if the final close reports failure.

examples.title: Core concept
examples.explanation: Trace the operations and check the relevant C standard library contracts and failure cases.

examples.title: Apply the concept safely
examples.code:
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) { FILE *f = fopen("safe.txt", "w"); if (!f) return 1; const char *text = "user supplied text"; int ok = fprintf(f, "%s\n", text) >= 0; if (fclose(f) == EOF) ok = 0; return ok ? 0 : 1; }
examples.explanation: This example reinforces the topic with explicit validation or resource handling. Compile with warnings and test failure paths.

practise.guidedTask: Create a small C program demonstrating Writing text and formatted data to files. Write down its preconditions, expected result and failure handling before implementation.
practise.independentTask: Extend the example for Writing text and formatted data to files to handle a boundary case and an error case. Explain the relevant C rule and add a test for each path.
hints: Read the declaration and function contract carefully.
Check all library return values before using results.
Keep object bounds, lifetime and resource ownership explicit.
Do not assume implementation-specific memory or file representations are portable.
Test both success and failure paths.

questions.prompt: Which function writes a null-terminated string to a stream?
questions.explanation: fputs writes a string to the selected stream.

questions.prompt: What should be checked after fprintf?
options: Its return value for an output error
questions.answer: Its return value for an output error
questions.explanation: fprintf reports output failure through its return value.

questions.prompt: Why can a successful write call be followed by a close failure?
options: Output may be buffered until later
questions.answer: Output may be buffered until later
questions.explanation: The final flush can reveal a delayed I/O error.

questions.prompt: Which is the safer way to write untrusted text?
questions.explanation: The format string remains a trusted constant; user text is treated as data.

questions.prompt: Which format specifier is appropriate for size_t?
questions.explanation: The z length modifier is used for size_t with the u conversion.
